title: Hotels Near Tokyo With Indoor Pools You Can Actually Use in Winter
description: Almost every hotel pool in Japan closes by mid-September. If you are travelling with kids outside summer — or want a rainy-day backup — these are the hotels near Tokyo with heated indoor pools open all year, and what to check before you book.
intro: Here is something that surprises a lot of families visiting Japan: booking a hotel “with a pool” is no guarantee you can swim. Most hotel pools here are outdoor and seasonal, opening in early July and closing by mid-September — so a hotel that advertises its pool in photos may have it drained and fenced off when you arrive in October. If you are travelling outside summer, you need a hotel with a heated indoor pool that runs year-round, and there are fewer of them within reach of Tokyo than you would expect. This guide lists them in the order that makes sense for overseas visitors — weighting ease of access and English-language service, which is not the order a Japanese guide would use. Two practical things to sort out before you book: whether the pool costs extra on top of your room, and whether the hotel prices per room or per person. Both are covered below.
listHeading: Hotels near Tokyo with year-round indoor pools

buyingGuide.title: Check that the pool is indoor and open year-round — not just that it exists
buyingGuide.body: This is the whole problem in one sentence. Most outdoor hotel pools near Tokyo run from early July to early or mid-September, and some close earlier in bad weather, but the marketing photos stay up all year. A listing that says “pool” tells you nothing about October. What you are looking for specifically is a heated indoor pool with year-round operation, which is a much smaller set of hotels. Confirm it on the hotel's own site rather than on a booking platform's amenity list, since those are frequently generic and do not distinguish between indoor and seasonal outdoor facilities.

buyingGuide.title: “Hotel with a pool” often means “pool for an extra fee”
buyingGuide.body: In many Japanese city hotels the pool is part of a fitness club or spa rather than a free guest facility, and using it costs extra — sometimes several thousand yen per person per day. Resort hotels aimed at families more often include access in the room rate, but not always, and some run time-slot systems. There are also restrictions that matter with young children: minimum age or height limits, whether babies in swim nappies are allowed, and whether armbands and inflatable rings can be brought in. Look up the fee and the age rules for your actual dates, since both change seasonally.

buyingGuide.title: Japanese resorts price per person, with dinner and breakfast included
buyingGuide.body: This catches out almost every first-time visitor comparing prices. International-style hotels quote per room, as you would expect at home. Traditional and domestic spa resorts — including several below — quote per person, and the rate normally includes both dinner and breakfast, often a large buffet. So a resort showing a much higher number may actually be cheaper for a family of four once you account for eight meals. When comparing options here, work out the total for your whole party including food, not the headline figure.

buyingGuide.title: The pool and the onsen are different facilities with different rules
buyingGuide.body: Several hotels here pair the pool with an onsen — a hot spring bath complex — and they are not interchangeable. The pool is mixed-gender and you wear swimwear. The onsen is segregated by gender and bathed in naked, with no swimwear permitted, and you wash thoroughly at the shower stations before getting in. On a cold day the appeal is doing them in sequence: swim, then warm up in the baths. Worth knowing that rules on tattoos, where they apply at all, are usually stricter for the onsen than for the pool, and vary by property — if you have larger tattoos it is worth a quick check with the hotel.

buyingGuide.title: An indoor pool is your best rainy-day insurance
buyingGuide.body: Beyond off-season swimming, a year-round indoor pool solves a specific problem: what to do with children on a wet day. Japan's rainy season runs roughly through June, typhoons can arrive between August and October, and winter brings cold, short days. Outdoor sightseeing plans fall apart quickly in any of these. If your itinerary already includes a fixed multi-night stay near Tokyo, putting it at a hotel with an indoor pool costs little and turns a written-off day into an easy one.

places.name: Hilton Tokyo Bay
places.area: Urayasu, Chiba · about 30–40 minutes from Tokyo Station
places.description: The most straightforward choice for overseas families, and the one we would book first. It is an official Tokyo Disney Resort hotel on the bay, with an indoor pool open year-round plus a separate outdoor pool in summer — so unlike most hotels in the area, the swimming does not disappear in September. Being a Hilton, English-language service and international expectations around check-in, breakfast and family rooms are a given, which removes a lot of friction if this is your first trip to Japan. It is also enormous and consistently well reviewed by domestic guests, with over 13,000 reviews on Japanese booking sites averaging around 4.4 out of 5. Best if you are combining Disney with a Tokyo trip and want the fewest surprises.
pros: Year-round indoor pool plus a seasonal outdoor pool
Official Disney Resort hotel with shuttle access to the parks
International-brand service and reliable English support
cons: Pool hours and access rules vary by season — confirm for your dates
Very busy during Japanese school holidays and Disney peak periods

places.name: The Prince Park Tower Tokyo
places.japaneseName: ザ・プリンス パークタワー東京
places.area: Shiba Park, central Tokyo · at the foot of Tokyo Tower
places.description: The pick if you want to stay central rather than out on the bay. This is a luxury hotel in Shiba Park directly beneath Tokyo Tower, with an indoor pool inside its spa complex that operates year-round. Staying here means you are inside Tokyo proper — walking distance to Tokyo Tower and Zojoji Temple, with the subway network at your door — so the pool becomes an evening wind-down or a rainy-morning option rather than the reason for the trip. It rates close to 4.5 out of 5 with domestic reviewers. Worth knowing before you book: because the pool sits within the spa, access is commonly charged separately and may carry age restrictions, which makes it a better fit for couples and older children than for toddlers.
pros: Genuinely central location with excellent transport links
Year-round indoor pool within a full spa complex
High-end facilities suited to a special-occasion stay
cons: Pool access is often charged separately and may restrict young children
The most expensive option here by a clear margin

places.name: Ryugujo Spa Hotel Mikazuki
places.japaneseName: 龍宮城スパ・ホテル三日月 龍宮亭
places.area: Kisarazu, Chiba · about 45–60 minutes by bus from Tokyo Station
places.description: If the pool is the point of the trip, this is the one. The hotel's indoor “Aqua Park” is a full water complex rather than a single lap pool, combined with an extensive onsen, and it runs year-round regardless of weather. The draw is being able to swim and then move straight into hot spring baths — exactly what you want on a cold day, and something no city hotel here can offer. It reaches Tokyo quickly via the Tokyo Bay Aqua-Line, the bridge-tunnel across the bay, so it feels much further from the city than it is. Best for families who want one day where nobody has to leave the building. Be aware it is a domestic resort: English-language support is more limited, and it gets genuinely crowded on weekends and holidays.
pros: A large indoor water complex, not just a swimming pool
Swim and then use the onsen without going outside
Surprisingly quick to reach from central Tokyo via the Aqua-Line
cons: Limited English-language support compared with international chains
Crowded at weekends and during Japanese holiday periods

places.name: Nikko Kinugawa Hotel Mikazuki
places.japaneseName: 日光きぬ川ホテル三日月
places.area: Kinugawa Onsen, Tochigi · about 2 hours from Asakusa
places.description: The best option if you are already going to Nikko, which many visitors are — Toshogu Shrine and the surrounding national park are among the most rewarding trips out of Tokyo. This large riverside resort has an indoor pool and a varied set of hot spring baths under one roof in its “Ryugu Spa”, so it works year-round and pairs naturally with a shrine visit rather than requiring a separate trip. Rooms tend to cost less than comparable places in Hakone. The trade-off is the journey: roughly two hours by direct limited express from Asakusa, and the town itself is quiet after dark, so plan to spend your evening inside the hotel. Autumn is the standout season here, when the gorge turns colour.
pros: Combines easily with Nikko's UNESCO shrines and national park
Indoor pool and multiple hot spring baths in one complex
Better value than equivalent resorts closer to Tokyo
cons: About two hours each way — not a quick side trip
Little to do in the surrounding town in the evening

places.name: Hotel New Otani Makuhari
places.japaneseName: ホテルニューオータニ幕張
places.area: Makuhari, Chiba · about 30 minutes from Tokyo Station
places.description: The value choice, and a practical base if your trip involves Narita Airport or an event at Makuhari Messe, the large convention centre next door. The indoor pool in the hotel's fitness and spa area is open year-round, with an outdoor garden pool added in summer. Rates are noticeably lower than the Tokyo and bayside options while the hotel itself is large and well equipped, and it holds close to 4.4 out of 5 across several thousand domestic reviews. Makuhari is a planned business and shopping district rather than a sightseeing destination, so this is a hotel you choose for convenience and price rather than atmosphere. As with most city hotels, check whether pool access carries a separate charge.
pros: Clearly cheaper than the central Tokyo and Disney-area options
Year-round indoor pool, plus an outdoor pool in summer
Convenient for Narita Airport and Makuhari Messe events
cons: Pool access may cost extra — confirm before booking
The area is business and shopping oriented, with little sightseeing

places.name: Hotel Epinard Nasu
places.japaneseName: ホテルエピナール那須
places.area: Nasu, Tochigi · about 70 minutes by Shinkansen, then a shuttle
places.description: A highlands resort with a strong domestic following, and the most family-oriented property here — but also the furthest and the least geared toward overseas guests. Its heated indoor pool runs year-round, alongside natural hot springs and a substantial set of children's facilities, on a large site in the Nasu highlands. Domestic families rate it highly, with more than 8,000 reviews averaging around 4.4 out of 5. The reason it sits last is logistics rather than quality: reaching Nasu means a Shinkansen to Nasushiobara plus a shuttle, which is a lot of movement for a short trip and hard to justify unless you are staying two nights or more. Consider it if you want a genuine Japanese family resort and have the time in your itinerary.
pros: Year-round heated indoor pool with natural hot springs
Extensive children's facilities — easy to fill a full day on site
Highly rated by domestic families across 8,000+ reviews
cons: The longest and most awkward journey of the six
Very much a domestic resort — expect limited English

faq.question: When do outdoor hotel pools in Japan actually close?
faq.answer: Most outdoor pools near Tokyo operate from early July to early or mid-September only, and some close earlier in poor weather. This is why a hotel can advertise a pool you cannot use during your stay — the photos are from the summer season. If you are travelling from mid-September onward, or in spring, do not rely on a listing simply saying “pool”. Confirm specifically that the hotel has an indoor pool and that it runs year-round, ideally on the hotel's own website rather than a booking platform.

faq.question: Is pool access included in the room rate?
faq.answer: Not always, and it varies by hotel type. Family-focused resorts more often include it, while city hotels frequently run the pool as part of a fitness club or spa with a separate daily charge — occasionally several thousand yen per person. Some also use time-slot systems, or set minimum ages and height limits that affect younger children. Check the specific fee, opening hours and age rules for your travel dates, since these change seasonally.

faq.question: Are these hotels priced per room or per person?
faq.answer: It depends on the type. International-style hotels such as Hilton Tokyo Bay, The Prince Park Tower Tokyo and Hotel New Otani Makuhari generally price per room, as you would expect at home. The Japanese spa resorts — the two Mikazuki properties and Hotel Epinard Nasu — usually price per person and include dinner and breakfast in the rate, often as a large buffet. Their headline figures look high by comparison until you account for two meals for everyone in your party, at which point they can work out cheaper for a family.

faq.question: What is the difference between the pool and the onsen?
faq.answer: They are separate facilities with different rules. The pool is mixed-gender and you wear swimwear, as you would anywhere else. The onsen is a hot spring bath, segregated by gender, and bathed in naked — swimwear is not permitted, and you wash thoroughly at the shower stations before entering. Several hotels here have both, and the appeal on a cold day is doing them in sequence: swim first, then warm up in the baths. Where tattoo restrictions apply, they are generally stricter for the onsen than for the pool.

faq.question: Do I need to bring anything specific for the pool?
faq.answer: Bring normal swimwear and check the individual hotel's page for anything unusual. Requirements vary between properties: a few pools ask for swim caps, some limit inflatable rings and armbands, and rules on babies in swim nappies differ. Towels are usually provided at hotel pools, though not always at the poolside itself. None of this is difficult, but a two-minute look at the hotel's pool page before you travel avoids the one scenario worth avoiding — arriving at the pool and being turned away.

faq.question: Which of these is best if I only have one night?
faq.answer: Hilton Tokyo Bay or The Prince Park Tower Tokyo. Both are close enough to central Tokyo that you are not spending half your stay in transit, and both have reliable English-language service. Choose the Hilton if you have children or Disney plans, and the Prince Park Tower if you want to stay central and sightsee on foot. The Mikazuki resorts and Hotel Epinard Nasu are better suited to two nights or more, since the journey takes up a meaningful share of a single-night stay.
